title: MMReD: Cross-Modal Dense Context Reasoning Benchmark
one_liner: A benchmark that measures how well language and vision models can reason over dense, packed contexts where simple searching does not work.
lead: Current language and vision models can read long documents, but they struggle to understand patterns across all the information. This benchmark tests whether models can truly reason over dense contexts — situations where every piece of information matters and you need to see how things connect globally, not just pluck out one needle from a haystack.

problem.h2: Why context length alone is not enough
paras: Today's language models can handle very long input texts — thousands or even tens of thousands of words. But long input does not mean they understand the whole picture. The classic test, Needle-in-a-Haystack, just hides one fact in a pile of words and asks the model to find it. This is easy retrieval: scan the pile, spot the needle.

Real reasoning over dense contexts is different. It means noticing patterns that emerge only when you look at ALL the pieces together — how three pieces of information contradict each other, where a concept repeats across different sections, how a trend evolves as you move through the data. A naive model just tries to use its usual retrieval tricks and misses the global picture.

callout.html: The benchmark tests whether models can detect patterns and relationships across all the information, not just retrieve isolated facts.

steps.text: Tasks range from simple retrieval to reasoning that requires the model to focus on all chunks.
Some tasks need to focus on key chunks only; others demand equal focus across all sections.
Test each task with 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, and 128 chunks of dense information.

steps.b: Run all models through the gauntlet
steps.text: Evaluate language models, vision-language models, reasoning specialists, code models.
Record how accuracy drops as context grows. Identify which tasks break first.

paras: The benchmark itself — the measurement tool — changes what we test. Instead of asking only "can the model find one needle?", it asks "can the model reason across all the context at once?".

hidden.h2: Dense reasoning capacity: the hidden quantity
hidden.name: How well a model reasons over all information at once
paras: Dense reasoning capacity is not the same as context window length. A model might accept 100,000 individual numbers from its input but fail to reason over patterns that require looking at all of them together. This benchmark measures the gap between input capacity and actual reasoning ability — how well can a model reason when it sees the full picture?

The paper estimates this by running tasks of increasing complexity at increasing context lengths and watching where accuracy falls. When a model gets 95% on a task with 4 chunks but 5% with 128 chunks, that gap is the limit of its dense reasoning. The benchmark also separates two types: selective reasoning (attending to only key chunks) versus uniform reasoning (needing to weigh everything equally).

heat.caption: Darker means tasks or contexts that fail harder. Marked cells show where the biggest gaps appear.

reads.html: Dense reasoning capacity is the ability to notice patterns only visible when you examine all the information together, not just retrieve isolated facts.
The benchmark operationalizes dense reasoning via 24 tasks with task-specific complexity levels tested across context lengths 4 to 128 chunks; performance drop measures reasoning degradation.

mechanism.h2: Why it reveals the hidden limit
paras: Models are built to do retrieval well: find the query, scan the context, pluck out the answer. When context is short, this works even if the task is not really retrieval — the model gets lucky by accident. But when all 128 chunks matter and no simple keywords pinpoint the answer, the model has to hold and weigh information across the entire input. It collapses because its architecture was never trained to maintain coherent reasoning over such dense global patterns.

The benchmark forces a choice: either the model has learned to reason globally (and succeeds even at 128 chunks) or it has only learned retrieval (and fails as context grows). The 24 tasks are designed to rule out shortcuts — each one demands that the model actually process and integrate information from many chunks at once, not just spot a surface signal.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Model A on a reasoning task: 95% accuracy with 4 chunks, 50% with 128 chunks. Gap = 95 - 50 = 45 percentage points.
Model B on the same task: 88% accuracy with 4 chunks, 15% with 128 chunks. Gap = 88 - 15 = 73 percentage points.
Model B loses more ability as context grows, so it has weaker dense reasoning capacity than Model A.
The benchmark reveals which models have learned true reasoning (small gap) versus clever retrieval only (large gap).

math.note: The bigger the accuracy drop, the less the model can reason over the full dense context.

charts.title: Passkey retrieval (simple search)
charts.note: Even simple retrieval starts to fail. Most models still do okay here.

charts.title: Selective reasoning (key chunks matter more)
charts.note: Performance collapses. Selective focusing does not scale.

charts.title: Uniform reasoning (all chunks matter equally)
charts.note: Complete failure at scale. Models cannot maintain global reasoning.

items.html: At 4-8 chunks, a model can succeed by pure surface matching even if it has no real reasoning ability. The benchmark designs tasks with no retrieval shortcuts — you must attend to the full context.
When a model must weigh 128 chunks equally, its ability to focus gets spread too thin. Each chunk receives minimal focus, and global patterns are lost in noise.

items.b: Fine-tuning does not fix the gap.
items.html: Even when trained on data with longer contexts, models do not generalize to tasks they have not seen before. The underlying architecture cannot handle dense reasoning.
Even models trained to reason do not escape the benchmark. This shows the problem is architectural, not just a matter of training technique.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small dense reasoning task: give a language model a set of 4, 8, 16, and 32 text chunks. Each chunk describes one person's opinions on three topics (e.g., climate, energy, economy). The task is to answer a question that requires detecting a pattern across all chunks — for example, "Who favors economic growth in the most topics?" Track accuracy as the number of chunks increases.
demo.closing: The demo will show that as context grows, even advanced models fall from high accuracy to near-random guessing, proving that they are not truly reasoning over the full context.
